The business of the petitioners with the complainant is not today but is close to more than a generation i.e., 2009-10.
4.
The parties to the lis have marketed several products and have claimed certain amounts.
Problems crop up in the year 2020 when certain amount is claimed by the complainant from the hands of the petitioners.
Initially, a legal notice comes to be issued by the complainant seeking certain amount narrating all the invoices and claiming an amount of Rs.7,12,92,625/-.
This is replied to by the petitioner contending NC: 2023:KHC:21188 that he is entitled to deduction of incentive at every point in time and what he has not paid to the complainant is the incentive.

After the reply to the legal notice, the respondent - complainant seeks to set the criminal law into motion by registering a complaint on 22.02.2022 alleging that the petitioners have not paid an amount of Rs.7,12,92,625/-, which amounts to offences under Sections 406 and 420 of IPC inter alia.
The complaint then becomes a crime, in Crime No.76/2022 for the afore-quoted offences.
Registration of a crime against the petitioners is what drives the petitioners to this Court in the subject petition.
5. This Court entertaining the petition had granted an interim order of stay on 30.06.2022 and the same is subsisting even as on date.

6. Learned counsel for the petitioners would contend with vehemence, that a issue is purely civil in nature is sought to be given a colour of crime, by setting the criminal law in motion, for the offences punishable under Sections 406 and 420 of IPC as the case would be.

He would take this Court through the documents appended to the petition i.e., legal NC: 2023:KHC:21188 notice, caused upon them and the reply submitted by them, with regard to the claim of detention, of the said amount which is the incentive according to the petitioners.
He would seek quashment of the entire proceedings on the score that a civil suit for recovery ought to have been filed, instead, the petitioners have preferred to set the criminal law in motion.
7. Learned counsel for the respondent would refute the submissions to contend that it clearly amounts to criminal breach of trust as obtaining under Section 406 of IPC.
Therefore, would submit that it is a matter of trial for the petitioners to come out clean.

He would further admit that the complainants would undoubtedly initiate civil proceedings for recovery of money as an amount of Rs.7,12,92,625/- is what is to be paid from the petitioners to the respondent - Company.
He would seek dismissal of the petition contenting that it is for the petitioners to come out clean in the further investigation or the trial as the case would be.
8. I have given my anxious consideration to the contentions of respective learned counsel and have perused the material on record.
The aforesaid facts are not in dispute.
It is not in dispute that the petitioners are a proprietorship concern that markets the products manufactured by the second respondent.
The relationship of business between the petitioners and the complainant dates back to 2009-10.
From 2009-10, upto the date of causing of the legal notice, the business appears to be smooth sailing.

In fact, in the discussion that you had with our client in June 2020, you had assured payments towards the outstanding sums by 15 November 2020.
5. Our client instructs us to state that even though you had assured payments by 15 November 2020, you failed to do so.
When our client approached you once against with a request to make payments towards the monies due, you made some frivolous allegations to withhold payments.
Having received the goods and evidently having sold the same subsequently, it is not open to you withhold payments.
In the tight of your stand, our client had made it clear that you should either make payments or return the good purchased.
The frivolousness of your allegations was evident when you refused to return the goods.

6. Our Client has patiently waited for the realization of outstanding amounts and has made several attempts to reach out to you vide reminder emails dated 18 December 2020, 23 December 2020, 30 December 2020, 08 January 2021, 25 March 2021, and 01 April 2021.

Despite repeated follow-ups, you have neither replied to the said NC:
2023:KHC:21188 emails nor sought to return the goods purchased or make the payment towards the amounts due.

You are liable to make payment to the tune of INR 7,12,92,625/- (Seven Crores Twelve Lakhs Ninety- Two Thousand six Hundred and Twenty Five Rupees only) which is reflecting as per the Closing Balance in the books of accounts of our Client as on 31 March 2021.
In addition, our client is also entitled to receive interest on the outstanding amounts.

7. In view of the foregoing, our Client calls upon you to forthwith pay a sum of INR 7,12,92,625/- along with interest at 18% per annum, within 15 days from the date of the notice, failing which our Client would proceed to initiate legal proceedings for recovery of the outstanding amounts.

8. Please note that this Notice for recovery of outstanding dues is being issued without prejudice to all rights, prerogatives, and remedies available to our Client under law."

sentences.text: the complainant is that there is criminal breach of trust.
Section 406 of IPC has its ingredients in Section 405 of IPC.

Section 405 of IPC reads as follows:
" 405. Criminal breach of trust.--Whoever, being in any manner entrusted with property, or with any dominion over property, dishonestly misappropriates or converts to his own use that property, or dishonestly uses or disposes of that property in violation of any direction of law prescribing the mode in which such trust is to be - 13 - NC: 2023:KHC:21188 discharged, or of any legal contract, express or implied, which he has made touching the discharge of such trust, or wilfully suffers any other person so to do, commits "criminal breach of trust".
Section 405 of IPC mandates that there should entrustment of property, misappropriation of such entrustment with dishonest intention should happen, it is then, it would become an offence under Section 406 of IPC.
13. Insofar as Section 420 of IPC is concerned, Section 420 of IPC has its ingredients in Section 415 of IPC.

Section 415 of IPC reads as follows:
" 415. Cheating.--Whoever, by deceiving any person, fraudulently or dishonestly induces the person so deceived to deliver any property to any person, or to consent that any person shall retain any property, or intentionally induces the person so deceived to do or omit to do anything which he would not do or omit if he were not so deceived, and which act or omission causes or is likely to cause damage or harm to that person in body, mind, reputation or property, is said to "cheat".
Section 415 of IPC mandates that the accused should have lured the victim to part any property with dishonest intention right from the beginning of the transaction. The - 14 - NC: 2023:KHC:21188 transaction between the two are the proprietorship concern markets the products that are manufactured by the complainant, and it is not today but in decade, the transaction between the two, is go on.

The dispute is with regard to the claim of Rs.7,12,92,625/-
and the justification of the petitioners is that he is entitled to an incentive which he has withheld.

With this justification and the dispute, I fail to understand as to how it would amount to criminal breach of trust or even cheating as obtaining under Sections 405 or 415 of IPC, which can become punishable under Sections 406 or 420 of IPC.
14.
Learned counsel for the respondent rightly submits that they would initiate proceedings for recovery of the amounts.
Therefore, it is for the respondent - complainant to avail of such remedy as is available in law by initiating any proceeding seeking recovery of money.
